items.title: UK GDPR, Article 35: Data protection impact assessment
items.quote: Where necessary, the controller shall carry out a review to assess if processing is performed in accordance with the data protection impact assessment
items.why: The binding rule: assess before high-risk processing (35(1)), minimum contents (35(7)), review when the risk changes (35(11)). The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 did not alter the duty; the only change since 2020 is 'Commission' in 35(4) and (5), substituted 30 September 2026 by S.I. 2026/386. No outstanding changes shown on the day checked.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 83: General conditions for imposing administrative fines
items.quote: the obligations of the controller and the processor pursuant to Articles 8, 11, 25 to 39 and 42 and 43
items.why: Places Article 35 in the lower of the two penalty tiers. The amount is not repeated in the brief because another brief already uses it.

items.title: Data protection impact assessments: What is a DPIA?
items.quote: a DPIA is not simply a rubber stamp or a technicality as part of a sign-off process
items.why: States that outcomes must be integrated back into the project plan and that the assessment is a 'living' process to be reviewed when anything changes. Carries the 'under review' banner following the Data (Use and Access) Act; no date on the page, so the year is the year read.

items.title: Data protection impact assessments: When do we need to do a DPIA?
items.locator: Sections 'What other factors might indicate likely high risk?' and 'What does the ICO consider likely to result in high risk?'
items.quote: In most cases, a combination of two of these factors indicates the need for a DPIA.
items.why: The screening test. Lists the regulator's ten extra triggers; innovative technology (including AI) requires an assessment when combined with one other criterion, and automated decisions on access to a service require one outright. Says a decision not to assess should be documented. 'Under review' banner; undated page.

items.title: Data protection impact assessments: How do we do a DPIA?
items.locator: Sections 'Step 7: How do we conclude our DPIA?' and 'What happens next?'
items.quote: You should identify any action points and who is responsible for implementing them.
items.why: The regulator's seven steps and what happens after sign-off: outcomes go into the project plan, actions have owners, the assessment is kept under review. It asks for an owner per action; it does not ask for dates or closure evidence. 'Under review' banner; undated page.

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: What are the accountability and governance implications of AI?
items.locator: Section 'What do we need to consider when undertaking data protection impact assessments for AI?'
items.quote: the use of AI will involve a type of processing likely to result in a high risk to individuals’ rights and freedoms
items.why: Source of the statement that the great majority of AI uses trigger the duty, and that a decision that a use is not high risk must still be documented. Asks for evidence of less risky alternatives considered, and for review as populations and behaviour shift. 'Under review' banner; latest update shown is 15 March 2023.

items.title: AI tools in recruitment: audit outcomes report
items.quote: AI providers had completed DPIAs retrospectively or just prior to the audit
items.why: What the regulator found when it read real assessments: some done after the fact, some undated, many lacking necessity and alternatives, few recording what changed after consultation, most not regularly reviewed once the tool was live (p. 36). Findings are qualitative; no counts are given for this section.

items.title: Decision of the Information Commissioner: Snap Inc. and Snap Group Limited
items.quote: a cursory and higher-level risk assessment, in tabular format
items.why: Source of the quotation and the figure. A preliminary enforcement notice (6 October 2023) alleged breach of Articles 35 and 36; the firm produced a fifth assessment on 22 November 2023, which was accepted, so no enforcement notice was issued and no infringement was finally found. Shows the regulator reading an assessment line by line against Article 35(7). Redacted public version.

items.title: Guidelines on Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) and determining whether processing is "likely to result in a high risk" for the purposes of Regulation 2016/679 (WP 248 rev.01)
items.publisher: Article 29 Data Protection Working Party (European Commission)
items.locator: Section III.D(a), p. 14; nine criteria at pp. 9-11; Annex 2 (criteria for an acceptable DPIA)
items.quote: Carrying out a DPIA is a continual process, not a one-time exercise.
items.why: The European guidelines that the UK regulator's trigger list is built on, and whose Annex 2 it recommends as a quality checklist. Not binding in the UK since exit; the UK regulator says such guidelines may still be helpful.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), Article 27: Fundamental rights impact assessment for high-risk AI systems
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: include cross-references to the relevant sections of that data protection impact assessment
items.why: International comparator: a second assessment for certain deployers of high-risk systems (public bodies, private providers of public services, and deployers of the systems in points 5(b) and (c) of Annex III), which may draw on the data protection assessment. This is the Commission's copy, not the Official Journal; it carries a notice that the provision was amended by the Digital Omnibus and may not be fully updated. Paragraphs 4 and 5 are marked 'AMENDED'. No application date is stated here.
